title: Two questions that are not "what happens next"
abstract: 18. Two questions that are not "what happens next". EQUILIBRIUM (KINSOL) asks where the system comes to REST. SENSITIVITY (CVODES/IDAS) asks how much the answer DEPENDS on an input.
situation:
### The objects

| name | shape | given properties |
|---|---|---|
| `pivot` **(static)** | `sphere` | `mass = 1`, `radius = 0.02`, `position = [0, 0, 0]`, `inverse_mass = 0` |
| `bob` | `sphere` | `mass = 1`, `radius = 0.05`, `position = [0.8414709848078965, -0.5403023058681398, 0]` |
| `stone` | `sphere` | `mass = 2`, `radius = 0.05`, `position = [0, 0, 0]`, `velocity = [1, 0, 0]` |

Each row is one rigid body. The simulator computes each body's inertia tensor from its shape; you never type an inertia tensor in.

### The shapes, and the inertia each implies

**`sphere`** — a uniform solid ball. `I = diag(2mr^2/5, 2mr^2/5, 2mr^2/5)` — isotropic, so every axis through the centre is a principal axis with the same moment. The only shape whose inertia tensor is unchanged by any rotation, which makes it the simplest collidable body.

### What each property means

- **`mass`** — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- **`radius`** — the radius, in metres.
- **`position`** — the centre of mass, as `[x, y, z]` in metres.
- **`inverse_mass`** — one over the mass. Setting it to **0** makes the body STATIC: no force can accelerate it. This is how a body is bolted to the world, and it is representable as a finite number, which infinite mass is not.
- **`velocity`** — the centre-of-mass velocity, as `[vx, vy, vz]` in metres per second. Setting it sets the linear momentum to `m * v`; the momentum is what the state vector actually carries.

### The interactions

- **Mutual gravity is OFF** (`g_constant = 0`). The simulator's default is 1, so this had to be said explicitly; without it, bodies that are supposed only to bounce or to be held by joints would also attract each other.
- **Uniform gravity** is `[0, -9.81, 0]` metres per second squared, applied to every body alike.
- **Contact is OFF**. Nothing here is meant to touch anything else, so the rootfinder is not armed.
- **2 joints** hold the bodies together. A joint is an exact geometric relation held for all time by constraint forces the solver computes — not a stiff spring.
eom:
There are 3 bodies. Each obeys Newton's and Euler's equations, both of which are **second order**:

```
m_i * d2(x_i)/dt2 = m_i g + J^T lambda

I_i * d(omega_i)/dt + omega_i x (I_i omega_i) = T_i
```

The `omega x (I omega)` term in Euler's equation is the gyroscopic term. It is what makes a tumbling body's spin axis wander even with no torque at all, and it is why rigid-body motion cannot be reduced to three independent rotations.

The forces on the right are:

- `m_i g` — the uniform field, here `g = [0, -9.81, 0]`
- `J^T lambda` — the constraint forces the joints generate. These are NOT written down by you: they are the Lagrange multipliers, solved for at every step so the joint equations hold exactly

and the torques `T_i` likewise carry a constraint part `J_omega^T lambda`, which is how a bearing resists being twisted out of line.
constraints:
**1. `constrain pivot bob` — 1 row.** The distance between the two centres is fixed. With no length given it freezes whatever separation the two bodies already have, so you position them and then tie them. The constraint equation is `g = |x_b - x_a| - L`, written on the distance and not on its square: the squared form is tidier algebraically and worse numerically, because its gradient scales with `L` and the corrector stops converging for `L` far from 1.

**2. `constrain off` — 1 row.** The distance between the two centres is fixed. With no length given it freezes whatever separation the two bodies already have, so you position them and then tie them. The constraint equation is `g = |x_b - x_a| - L`, written on the distance and not on its square: the squared form is tidier algebraically and worse numerically, because its gradient scales with `L` and the corrector stops converging for `L` far from 1.

**The arithmetic that decides whether this can be solved at all.** 2 non-static bodies give `6 x 2 = 12` degrees of freedom, against **2 constraint rows**, leaving `12 - 2 = 10` freedoms.

Those remaining freedoms are the motion the mechanism actually has. Some of them may be passive — a freedom nothing applies a force along simply stays where it started.

Every row is held at the position level (`g = 0`) **and** at the velocity level (`d(g)/dt = J u = 0`) at the same time. That is what the GGL formulation is for, and it is why these joints do not slowly come apart.
reduction:
**Sizing this particular problem.** There are 3 bodies, so the state vector `y` has

```
3 bodies x 13 numbers = 39 components
```

laid out as consecutive 13-number blocks in creation order, each holding position (3), linear momentum (3), orientation quaternion w-first (4), and angular momentum (3).

The 1 static body still occupies its 13 slots. Its inverse mass is zero, so its momentum-to-velocity map returns zero and it never moves — carried as constants rather than special-cased out of the layout.

On top of those 39 differential unknowns are the algebraic ones: one Lagrange multiplier `lambda` and one position-level multiplier `mu` for each of the 2 constraint rows, so

```
2 lambda + 2 mu = 4 algebraic unknowns
```

giving **43 unknowns in total**, solved as one implicit system.

**What is handed to the Rust SUNDIALS translation.**

There are no algebraic constraints, so the whole of the mechanics above is one first-order system

```
dy/dt = f(t, y),   y in R^39
```

handed to the pure-Rust translation of **CVODE** in Adams-Moulton mode: a variable-order, variable-step explicit-family method for non-stiff problems. This is the default, and it is the right choice for orbits and for anything smooth.

The right-hand side `f` unpacks `y` into bodies, computes every force and torque, and packs the derivatives back in the same 13-per-body order.

steps.title: Set up the world
steps.explain:
The next cell sends these 3 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`set system.g_constant = 0` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `g_constant` is the gravitational constant `G` used for the mutual attraction between every pair of bodies, `F = G m1 m2 / r^2`. **Its default is 1, not 0**, which catches people out: bodies rattling in a box also attract each other unless you say otherwise. Set it to 0 for a mechanism or a collision experiment; set it to a real value for an orbit.

The value expected here is `0`. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`set system.uniform_gravity = [0, -9.81, 0]` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `uniform_gravity` is a uniform gravitational field applied to every body, as `[gx, gy, gz]` in metres per second squared. This is the everyday 'g' of falling, entirely separate from the mutual attraction above.

The value expected here is `[0, -9.81, 0]`. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`collide off` disarms contact detection. Nothing in this model is meant to touch anything else, so leaving it on would have the solver arm a rootfinder hunting for impacts that never happen. The form is `COLLIDE [ON|OFF]`; with no argument it reports the current setting.

It prints the resulting state and the number of collidable pairs.
steps.code:
sim.do("set system.g_constant = 0")
sim.do("set system.uniform_gravity = [0, -9.81, 0]")
sim.do("collide off")

steps.title: Create the bodies
steps.explain:
The next cell sends these 2 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`new sphere` creates one rigid body whose shape is **a uniform solid ball**, named `pivot`. The general form is

```
new <shape> [as <name>] { <field> = <value>, ... }
```

Its inertia tensor is not typed in — the simulator computes it from the shape: `I = diag(2mr^2/5, 2mr^2/5, 2mr^2/5)` — isotropic, so every axis through the centre is a principal axis with the same moment. The only shape whose inertia tensor is unchanged by any rotation, which makes it the simplest collidable body.

The fields given here are:

- `mass = 1` — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- `radius = 0.02` — the radius, in metres.
- `position = [0, 0, 0]` — the centre of mass, as `[x, y, z]` in metres.
- `inverse_mass = 0` — one over the mass. Setting it to **0** makes the body STATIC: no force can accelerate it. This is how a body is bolted to the world, and it is representable as a finite number, which infinite mass is not.

Because `inverse_mass` is zero this body is **static**: no force can move it. It is part of the world, not part of the motion.

The command prints the name the simulator assigned, which is how you confirm the body exists.

---

`new sphere` creates one rigid body whose shape is **a uniform solid ball**, named `bob`. The general form is

```
new <shape> [as <name>] { <field> = <value>, ... }
```

Its inertia tensor is not typed in — the simulator computes it from the shape: `I = diag(2mr^2/5, 2mr^2/5, 2mr^2/5)` — isotropic, so every axis through the centre is a principal axis with the same moment. The only shape whose inertia tensor is unchanged by any rotation, which makes it the simplest collidable body.

The fields given here are:

- `mass = 1` — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- `radius = 0.05` — the radius, in metres.
- `position = [0.8414709848078965, -0.5403023058681398, 0]` — the centre of mass, as `[x, y, z]` in metres.

The command prints the name the simulator assigned, which is how you confirm the body exists.
steps.code:
sim.do("new sphere as pivot { mass = 1, radius = 0.02, position = [0, 0, 0], inverse_mass = 0 }")
sim.do("new sphere as bob { mass = 1, radius = 0.05, position = [0.8414709848078965, -0.5403023058681398, 0] }")

steps.title: Declare the joints
steps.explain:
The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`CONSTRAIN` declares a joint. Its form is

```
CONSTRAIN <a> <b> [length]
```

and it contributes **1 scalar constraint equation** to the system, leaving 5 of the 6 relative freedoms between the two bodies.

What it holds: the distance between the two centres is fixed.

With no length given it freezes whatever separation the two bodies already have, so you position them and then tie them. The constraint equation is `g = |x_b - x_a| - L`, written on the distance and not on its square: the squared form is tidier algebraically and worse numerically, because its gradient scales with `L` and the corrector stops converging for `L` far from 1.

Here it is applied to `pivot bob`. The pivot goes at the **midpoint of the two bodies' centres as they stand right now**, and is then remembered in each body's own frame — which is why bodies are positioned before they are joined. The command prints a confirmation naming the joint and its row count.

steps.title: Measure
steps.explain:
**A note carried over from the example this notebook pairs with:**

> Where does it rest? Straight down, one rod-length below the pivot.

The next cell sends these 2 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`equilibrium` solves for a rest state with KINSOL, the pure-Rust translation of SUNDIALS' nonlinear algebraic solver: it finds a configuration at which all the forces balance.

A completely free system has no isolated equilibrium at all — translate the whole thing and nothing changes — so at least one body must be pinned, and the command says so if none is.

---

`get` evaluates an expression and prints it. The form is `GET <expression>`, where an expression may name a body's field (`obj0.position`, `bob.velocity.x`), index into it, or combine several with arithmetic and the built-in functions `norm`, `normalize`, `dot`, `cross`, `sqrt` and the rest.

Here it evaluates:

```
bob.position
```

The corresponding Python call `sim.get(...)` returns the value as a Python object instead of printing it, which is what you want when the number is about to be used in a calculation.

steps.title: Declare the joints (2)
steps.explain:
**A note carried over from the example this notebook pairs with:**

> Now a free body, and the exact derivative of free fall:
> y(T) = y0 + v0*T + g*T^2/2, so dy/dg = T^2/2 = 4.5 at T = 3.

The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`CONSTRAIN` declares a joint. Its form is

```
CONSTRAIN <a> <b> [length]
```

and it contributes **1 scalar constraint equation** to the system, leaving 5 of the 6 relative freedoms between the two bodies.

What it holds: the distance between the two centres is fixed.

With no length given it freezes whatever separation the two bodies already have, so you position them and then tie them. The constraint equation is `g = |x_b - x_a| - L`, written on the distance and not on its square: the squared form is tidier algebraically and worse numerically, because its gradient scales with `L` and the corrector stops converging for `L` far from 1.

Here it is applied to `off`. The pivot goes at the **midpoint of the two bodies' centres as they stand right now**, and is then remembered in each body's own frame — which is why bodies are positioned before they are joined. The command prints a confirmation naming the joint and its row count.

steps.title: Choose the integrator
steps.explain:
The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`method adams` chooses the time integrator. The form is `METHOD <adams|bdf|sprk|ida>`.

Here it selects the pure-Rust translation of **CVODE** in Adams-Moulton mode: a variable-order, variable-step explicit-family method for non-stiff problems. This is the default, and it is the right choice for orbits and for anything smooth.

All stepping in this simulator goes through the vendored pure-Rust SUNDIALS translation. There is no hand-written Euler or Verlet anywhere.

steps.title: Measure (3)
steps.explain:
The next cell sends these 2 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`sensitivity` computes derivatives of the trajectory with respect to a parameter, using CVODES and IDAS, the sensitivity-capable members of the SUNDIALS family. It answers 'how much would the answer move if this input moved', without re-running the whole simulation for each perturbed input.

---

`get` evaluates an expression and prints it. The form is `GET <expression>`, where an expression may name a body's field (`obj0.position`, `bob.velocity.x`), index into it, or combine several with arithmetic and the built-in functions `norm`, `normalize`, `dot`, `cross`, `sqrt` and the rest.

Here it evaluates:

```
stone.position
```

The corresponding Python call `sim.get(...)` returns the value as a Python object instead of printing it, which is what you want when the number is about to be used in a calculation.

discussion:
**What the cells above actually established.**

- The values printed above are the result. Read them against the physical expectations set out earlier in this notebook.

**How to judge a number here.** A disagreement with theory is only a defect if it fails to shrink when you ask for more accuracy. Tighten `system.rtol` and `system.atol` and re-run: a discretisation error converges, and a bug does not. The one place this does not apply is a model with orientation-gripping joints, where `rtol` is floored at `1e-6` and tightening past it buys nothing.

**The full note from the example this notebook pairs with**, which sets out why it was built this way:

EQUILIBRIUM (KINSOL) asks where the system comes to REST.
SENSITIVITY (CVODES/IDAS) asks how much the answer DEPENDS on an input.
